title: The Image Reconstruction Game: Drawing CommonGround Through Iterative Multimodal Dialogue

paper.title: The Image Reconstruction Game: Drawing Common Ground Through Iterative Multimodal Dialogue
paper.abstract:
Abstract We introduce the Image Reconstruction Game, a fully automated benchmark in which a vision-language model issues corrective instructions to an image generator across multiple turns, making accumulated common ground directly observable as a rendered image.
Benchmarking two Describer models crossed with two Generator models across seven image categories, we find that the describer is the dominant factor in reconstruction quality, while the generator determines whether iterative refinement helps or hurts. Mathematical and geometric images pose the greatest challenge. The describer’s token budget strongly affects convergence: shorter budgets yield sparser first renderings with more room for visible improvement, while longer budgets raise absolute quality but leave less to fix. Stronger describers use a richer correction vocabulary spanning spatial, numeric, and structural categories, while weaker describers concentrate on surface properties and tend to stop after a few turns. Human validation shows that the best automated judge reaches only slight-to-fair agreement with human preferences, and automated scores require human recalibration to be used reliably.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: In the IR game, one model (the describer) tries to steer another (the generator) towards faithful reproduction of a target, using only natural language descriptions, over several turns. Figure shows example of how the generated image develops in response to the instructions (which are not shown), for three different model pairings and the same target. Figure 2: Overview of the Image Reconstruction Game. The Describer (a VLM) has access to the target image I ∗ I^{*} and communicates with the Generator (an image model) exclusively through natural language. The Generator produces a rendering ( I 1 I_{1} or I 2 I_{2} ) from the accumulated dialogue; the Describer observes both I ∗ I^{*} and the rendering and issues a corrective instruction for the next turn. Each rendering makes the current state of common ground directly visible, and the loop continues until the Describer signals convergence or a turn limit is reached. Comparison is done between target image I ∗ I^{*} and the final turn generated image I T I_{T} . Imagine you have a picture “in your head” – a scene that you saw, a diagram that you think could explain something, etc. – that you want to see materialised. Image generation models aim to address this use case: You describe what is “in your head” using language, and the model generates an image. Where early models technically simply were functions from textual prompts to images, modern models set up this task in a more iterative, incremental and dialogic way, where earlier attempts can be corrected and modified. Using terminology from the study of conversations, this can be described as a process of conversational grounding Clark (1996) , where common ground between the interactants is reached through an interactive process of clarification and correction. This paper uses this setup to test current models on the various components of this task: How good are current language and vision models at describing an image in such a way as to steer an image generation model to reproduce it, and how good are such image generation models at being steered? Figure 1 illustrates the outputs of three model pairs across turns to reconstruct the target image through dialogue. This adds a new dimension to the testing of models that combine linguistic and visual capabilities, as commonly the focus in their evaluation is on non-interactive tasks—captioning, VQA, image–text alignment—that do not test the capacities Shridhar et al. (2020) . Settings such as those used in CoDraw ( Kim et al., 2019 ) establish that iterative visual communication can be studied as a collaborative task with measurable outcomes, but rely on human players and fixed symbolic representations. Conversational image generation systems ( El-Nouby et al., 2019 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) place the human in the describer role, targeting user intent rather than evaluating the describer itself. Neither line holds one component fixed while varying the other, and neither connects communication trajectories to human perceptual judgements of outcomes. We introduce the Image Reconstruction Game , a fully automated multimodal dialogue game that fills these gaps (see Figure 2 ). A describer model (a VLM) observes a target image and must steer an image generator to reproduce it through a sequence of natural-language turns; at each turn the generator’s rendering makes the current state of common ground directly visible, and the describer observes both target and all renderings up to that point in the dialogue before issuing a corrective instruction. No human is in the loop: the game is played entirely between models under controlled, reproducible conditions. This design lets us investigate four research questions: RQ1 Can VLMs detect fine-grained perceptual differences between paired images and verbalise them as actionable, corrective instructions? RQ2 Do those instructions measurably reduce the difference between the target and the current rendering over turns? RQ3 Does the describer–generator pair build common ground progressively, as reflected in both automated similarity scores and human ratings? RQ4 Which automated image-similarity metrics best track human perceptual judgements in this setting? Addressing this last question is non-trivial: embedding-based similarity metrics are known to diverge substantially from human perceptual judgements ( Ghazanfari et al., 2024 ) , and LLM-based judges—while better correlated with human ratings than CLIP or BLIP in text-to-image settings ( Lu et al., 2023 ) —cannot be assumed to carry over to image reconstruction without direct empirical validation ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Marjieh et al., 2024 ) . Our contributions are: (i) a new task formulation and instance set spanning seven image categories that vary the difficulty of perception and verbalisation; (ii) a benchmark comparing two describer models against two generators, isolating describer quality from generator variation; (iii) a human similarity rating study on a stratified subset, together with an analysis of which automated metrics are most reliable proxies; and (iv) a qualitative analysis of what kinds of differences are hard to perceive or verbalise 1 1 1 https://github.com/clp-research/image-reconstruction-game .

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: CoDraw ( Kim et al., 2019 ) establishes the asymmetric Teller–Drawer paradigm for iterative visual reconstruction through multi-turn dialogue, and related work shows how common ground accumulates across turns when agents describe or identify shared images ( Haber et al., 2019 ; Clark et al., 2021 ; Madureira and Schlangen, 2023 ; Testoni and Fernández, 2024 ; Han and Schlangen, 2017 ) . Game-based frameworks have also been adopted as evaluation instruments for language and multimodal models: Chalamalasetti et al. (2023) systematise this for text-based chat models, and Hakimov et al. (2025) extend it to multimodal models with games probing reference resolution and image comparison ( Zhong et al., 2021 ; Mohapatra, 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Our game inherits this paradigm where players are VLM models as describer and generative image model as generator, making common ground directly observable as a rendered image at every turn. A broad family of systems generates or refines images through multi-turn natural language ( Ullah et al., 2022 ; El-Nouby et al., 2019 ; Lee et al., 2021 ; Wei et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . In all cases a human user provides instructions; the research question is how to build a better generative pipeline, not how to evaluate the instruction-giver. Co-creative drawing agents assist human sketchers in open-ended creative tasks ( Davis et al., 2016 ; Davis et al., 2017 ; Fan et al., 2019 ; Huang et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Ibarrola et al., 2024 ; Davis and Rafner, 2025 ) , while emergent communication research asks whether agents can evolve functional visual protocols through interaction ( Fernando et al., 2020 ; Mihai and Hare, 2021 ; Qiu et al., 2022 ; Vinker et al., 2025 ) . Both treat visual output as a communicative medium, but target artistic expression or protocol emergence rather than the fidelity of reconstruction by existing models. Human evaluation of generated images typically takes the form of pairwise preference judgements or direct similarity ratings, and is used as the ground-truth reference against which automated metrics are calibrated. Standard metrics such as SSIM, LPIPS, DINO, and CLIP are known to diverge from human mid-level perceptual judgements ( Ghazanfari et al., 2024 ) , and multimodal LLMs similarly under-perform humans on explicit visual similarity tasks ( Fu et al., 2024 ) . LipSim ( Ghazanfari et al., 2024 ) and LLMScore ( Lu et al., 2023 ) address this by providing provably robust perceptual similarity estimates and aligning metrics to human quality ratings respectively, while Marjieh et al. (2024) ; Marjieh et al. (2022) show that LLMs can approximate human similarity ratings across perceptual domains, though with systematic biases. We extend this line to image reconstruction, using human ratings to validate LLM judges that also participated as Describer models. Recent benchmarks specifically targeting mathematical and geometric visual perception—including MathOPEval ( Li et al., 2025 ) , GGBench ( Wei et al., 2026 ) , MATHGLANCE ( Sun et al., 2025 ) —consistently show that diagram-level geometric perception is a critical bottleneck in current VLMs. Where these benchmarks measure whether a model can read a geometric figure, the Image Reconstruction Game asks whether a model can articulate residual differences between two such figures—a harder, relational task. Our finding that Functions and Geometry categories pose the greatest challenge aligns with and extends this body of evidence to corrective, goal-directed communication.

sections.heading: Game description.
sections.text: The Image Reconstruction Game is a two-player dialogue game implemented within the clem framework for game-based model evaluation ( Chalamalasetti et al., 2023 ; Hakimov et al., 2025 ) . In this framework, a programmatic GameMaster instantiates each game episode with a given target image, manages turn-by-turn prompting of the two players, enforces the communication protocol, and records the episode for scoring. The two players occupy asymmetric roles with different information access and capabilities (see Figure 2 ). The Describer is a Vision-and-Language Model that has full access to the target image I ∗ I^{*} . Its goal is to produce natural-language utterances that guide the Generator toward a faithful visual reproduction of I ∗ I^{*} . The Generator is an image generation model that never observes I ∗ I^{*} directly; it can only perceive the accumulated dialogue history—the sequence of Describer utterances—and must render an image conditioned on that text. The game unfolds over multiple turns: at each turn the Describer observes both I ∗ I^{*} and the Generator’s previous rendering I t − 1 I_{t-1} ( t t stands for the turn index), then issues a corrective instruction or signals convergence; the Generator produces a new image based on the dialogue and previous rendering. This iterative structure operationalises the progressive building of common ground ( Alikhani and Stone, 2020 ) : each rendering I t I_{t} is a visible projection of the shared state constructed so far, and each Describer utterance is a grounding act that attempts to reduce the residual gap. The asymmetric information design—where only the Describer knows I ∗ I^{*} — mirrors the Teller–Drawer setup of CoDraw ( Kim et al., 2019 ) and multimodal dialogue games (referential, collaboration, spatial navigation) studied by Hakimov et al. (2025) , while extending them to open-ended natural-language communication with modern generative image models.

sections.heading: Capability tested.
sections.text: The game is designed to probe two interleaved capabilities that standard VLM benchmarks Agrawal et al. (2017) ; Yue et al. (2024) do not jointly assess. First, the Describer must perceive fine-grained differences between I ∗ I^{*} and I t − 1 I_{t-1} — a visual discrimination task that is considerably harder than captioning a single image and that demands sensitivity to spatial, metric, and relational properties. Second, it must verbalise those differences as specific corrective instructions for the Generator to act on, which requires goal-directed language production rather than generic scene description. The Generator, in turn, must interpret and act on incremental instructions while maintaining coherence with what has already been rendered. Jointly, these demands test whether a VLM can function as a goal-directed communicative agent in a closed-loop, multimodal setting.

sections.heading: 3.2 Prompts and communication protocol
sections.text: Each player’s messages must conform to the communication protocol so that the GameMaster can validate, parse, and relay them between players. An episode continues until one of three stopping criteria is met: (1) Player A signals convergence by producing a done action; (2) the maximum turn limit of T = 10 T{=}10 is reached; or (3) a player violates the protocol.

sections.heading: Player A (Describer).
sections.text: Player A is a VLM that receives the target image I ∗ I^{*} and the most recent Generator rendering I t − 1 I_{t-1} at every turn (on turn 1, only I ∗ I^{*} is available, as no rendering exists yet). The GameMaster presents these images with a prompt that asks Player A either to describe I ∗ I^{*} in sufficient detail for an image generator to reproduce it (turn 1), or to identify specific remaining differences between I ∗ I^{*} and I t − 1 I_{t-1} and issue a targeted corrective instruction (turns t > 1 t>1 ). Player A must wrap its output in <DESCRIPTION> … </DESCRIPTION> tags so that the GameMaster can parse and relay the message to Player B; a response consisting solely of done (without tags) signals convergence and ends the episode. A token budget of 200 tokens per turn is imposed to enforce concise, targeted corrections rather than exhaustive re-descriptions. The correction turns place a higher demand on visual reasoning than the initial description: corrections must be relational —specifying what is wrong relative to the current rendering—should focus on what to improve rather than descriptions of the image from scratch.

sections.heading: Player B (Generator).
sections.text: Player B is an image generation model that receives two inputs at each turn: the previous rendering I t − 1 I_{t-1} and the text message produced by Player A in the same turn. It does not have access to I ∗ I^{*} at any point; its only signal is the accumulated dialogue history together with the visual context of its own previous output. The GameMaster also passes the full sequence of prior Player A utterances alongside I t − 1 I_{t-1} , ensuring that compositional information established in early turns is not lost when later turns focus on local corrections. Player B’s sole output is a new rendered image I t I_{t} , which is then forwarded to Player A as the basis for the next turn. All prompt templates are given in Appendix C . sections.heading: Describer models.
sections.text: We evaluate a set of publicly available VLMs in the Describer role. Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct Yang et al. (2025) was run locally on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU and GPT-5.2 model was accessed via API. A fixed token budget of 200 tokens was used.

sections.heading: Generator models.
sections.text: We use two image generation models as generators: Gemini-3.1-nano-banana and GPT-Image-1.5 . Both are accessed via their respective image generation APIs in image-to-image conditioning mode: at each turn the Generator receives the previous rendering I t − 1 I_{t-1} together with the accumulated dialogue history, not merely the latest instruction. Calls are made with default sampling parameters; seeds are not fixed across turns (as neither API exposes turn-level seed control), so observed score changes across turns reflect a combination of conditioning behaviour and sampling stochasticity. Each Describer is evaluated against each Generator, yielding a Describer × \times Generator grid of results; the Generator is held fixed within each grid cell so that outcome differences are attributable to the Describer’s communicative quality rather than to rendering capability.

sections.heading: 4.2 Benchmark conditions
sections.text: The benchmark comprises 14 experiment conditions obtained by crossing seven instance categories with two difficulty levels, easy and hard . Each condition contains 10 episodes , yielding 140 episodes in total. The six categories are generated synthetically by prompting an LLM to produce Python code, the code is executed to obtain the target image (see Figure 22 in Appendix C ). Figure 3 shows representative target images. Simple Shapes contain coloured geometric primitives at specified positions; differences are visually salient but require precise spatial and color language. Geometry diagrams depict labelled figures and constructions with subtle metric differences. Functions show mathematical function graphs; differences concern curve shape, scale, and axis labels. Line Graph , Bar Graph , and Pie Graph encode statistical data visually; corrections must be numerically precise. We also use real photographs from the Visual Genome Krishna et al. (2017) dataset to compare the with synthetic categories. Difficulty is defined consistently across synthetic categories: easy instances use fewer elements, simpler structure, and unambiguous layouts, while hard instances introduce additional complexity—more data series, finer geometric detail, denser labelling—that increases both perceptual and verbalisation demands. For Visual Genome, easy instances depict scenes with a small number of salient objects; hard instances are denser and more cluttered. All instances were checked and verified manually (synthetic ones were generated with the complexity included in the prompt and then confirmed, Visual Genome instances were manually selected). Hard instances receive consistently lower mean similarity scores than easy instances across all categories and model pairs (Table 3 , Appendix B ), confirming the intended difficulty ordering.

sections.heading: 4.3 Tasks & Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate episode outcomes using two tasks.

sections.heading: Task 1: Pairwise Similarity
sections.text: Judges are shown the target image ( Image A ) and a Generator rendering ( Image B ) and asked to rate their visual and semantic similarity on a 0–10 scale: How similar is Image B to Image A? Image A is the original. Image B was generated by a model. Please rate their overall visual & semantic similarity using the scale below: 0 Completely different image 1–3 Very different; only a few elements in common 4–6 Partial match; some key elements captured, but important differences remain 7–9 Strong match; most elements correct, with minor differences in detail, colour, or placement 10 Identical or indistinguishable

sections.heading: Task 2: Triplet Preference
sections.text: Judges are shown the target image alongside two Generator renderings (from the first and the final turns) and asked to select which rendering is more visually similar to the target . This two-alternative forced-choice format abstracts away from absolute scale calibration and directly measures relative reconstruction quality—for example, whether a later-turn rendering is preferred over an earlier one considering the iterative improvement across turns.

sections.heading: Human judges.
sections.text: We collect human ratings for both tasks by asking them to annotate all 140 episodes. Each data point in both tasks is rated by three independent annotators with backgrounds in Computational Linguistics and Computer Science (who are also authors). The annotation guidelines and interfaces are given in Appendix A .

sections.heading: LLM judges.
sections.text: We use three LLMs as judges for both tasks. GPT-5.2 and Qwen3-VL-30B are drawn from the same model families used in the Describer role, allowing us to examine whether a model’s ratings are consistent with—or systematically biased by—its prior exposure to the task as a generator of descriptions. Self-serving evaluation, in which a model rates its own outputs more favourably than an independent observer would, is a known failure mode of LLM-as-judge pipelines ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Marjieh et al., 2024 ) ; including these models as judges provides a direct test of whether this bias is present in our setting. Claude-4.5 Sonnet was not used in experiments and therefore we included it as an independent, out-of-distribution LLM judge. Comparing the three judges against each other and against human ratings allows us to assess both the overall reliability of LLM-based evaluation in this setting and the degree to which judge scores are confounded by a model’s participation in the task being evaluated. sections.heading: Automated metrics.
sections.text: LipSim ( Ghazanfari et al., 2024 ) serves as the automated metric for Task 2; standard alternatives (SSIM, LPIPS, DINO, CLIP) are excluded as they are well-documented to diverge from human mid-level perceptual judgements ( Ghazanfari et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) . LipSim provides a provably robust perceptual similarity distance using Lipschitz-constrained neural networks, offering certified stability under input perturbations.

sections.heading: 5.2 Overall Performance
sections.text: Figure 4 shows mean similarity scores for all four describer–generator pairs (full breakdown in Table 3 , Appendix B ). The describer is the dominant factor (RQ1) : gpt-5.2 outperforms Qwen-3 by approximately one point across all conditions, with the ranking stable across all three judges. Within each describer, gemini-3.1 yields higher scores than gpt-image-1.5 ( RQ2 ). Category-level results reveal two separable bottlenecks: perception limits scores on Functions and Geometry hard instances (fine-grained details such as curve shapes, axis ticks), while verbalisation is the separate challenge of converting perceived differences into actionable instructions.

sections.heading: 5.3 Iterative Refinement
sections.text: The iterative payoff (the difference in scores between the final turn image in comparison to the first turn image) is as follows and address the RQ3 : Δ Q = score I T − score I 1 \Delta_{Q}=\text{score}_{I_{T}}-\text{score}_{I_{1}} . Gemini-3.1 pairings improve across turns; gpt-image-1.5 pairings show near-zero or negative deltas—additional turns degrade rather than improve the reconstruction (Figures 18 and 18 , Appendix B ). The generator also determines whether iterative refinement is beneficial . Figure 5 shows convergence outcomes per pair where each category refers to whether the first turn image has changed in scores in comparison to the final turn one. Qwen3-based pairs produce mostly single-turn episodes, leaving little room for improvement or regression; gpt-5.2 / gpt-image-1.5 continues to the turn limit but still regresses in roughly a third of cases. More turns do not guarantee higher quality (see also Figure 19 , Appendix B ). Among all pairs, gpt-5.2 + gemini-3.1 shows the most consistent per-turn improvement. sections.heading: 5.4 Describer Token Budget
sections.text: To analyse the effect of the token budget, we also ran gpt-5.2 + gpt-image-1.5 with 10, 50 tokens per turn to compare with 200 tokens experiments (see Figure 6 ). A shorter budget yields more visibly improved final images: at 10 tokens the first rendering I 1 I_{1} is sparse, so corrections have substantial room to close the gap; at 200 tokens I 1 I_{1} is already detailed, leaving little room for improvement—and more for regression. Absolute final-turn scores increase with budget while triplet preference for the final image decreases because it is easier to tell apart the first rendering from the final when the budget is low (full statistics in Figures 18 and 18 , Appendix B ). This quality–stability trade-off is driven by the starting-point quality of I 1 I_{1} . Figure 6: Convergence outcomes by token budget for gpt-5.2 + gpt-image-1.5 . A shorter budget produces a sparser first rendering, giving corrections more visible room to improve it.

sections.heading: 5.5 Correction Language
sections.text: We collected a list of words for respective categories that the describer uses to correct the rendering on subsequent turns. Figure 7 summarises the per-category usage rate per model pair. gpt-5.2 corrections are lexically broad, spanning Label/Text , Numeric , Comparison , and Positive Acknowledgement in addition to the universal Position and Color axes. Qwen3-VL-30B corrections concentrate almost exclusively on Color and Shape , with near-zero Numeric use (GPT-5.2 uses coordinate notation such as x=0 , y=0 ; Qwen3 contributes almost nothing) and zero Positive Acknowledgement . Qwen3-based pairs produce mostly single-turn episodes, so the language profile reflects only the coarsest initial instructions, with no opportunity for the structural and numeric precision that GPT-5.2 develops over longer dialogues (Table 5 : full list of keywords, Figure 14 : top-10 keywords). sections.heading: 5.7 Qualitative Analysis
sections.text: Qualitative samples are available in Figure 8 , Figure 9 , and Figure 10 for Functions , Geometry and Visual Genome instances. Across all three category types, gpt-5.2 + gemini-3.1 produces the closest renderings; gpt-5.2 + gpt-image-1.5 runs to ten turns but still falls short on fine details. Lower token budgets and Qwen3-based pairs yield semantically weaker reconstructions, with key structural elements missing or substituted.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced the Image Reconstruction Game, a fully automated multimodal reference game that turns common ground into a directly observable artefact: the rendered image produced after each dialogue turn. Unlike static benchmarks, the game separately measures two distinct model competencies—the ability to perceive and verbalise residual differences (Describer), and the ability to incorporate targeted corrections without losing prior progress (Generator). Our experiments show that describer quality is the dominant factor in reconstruction fidelity, while the generator determines whether multi-turn interaction provides any benefit at all. Notably, stronger VLMs are capable of fine-grained visual articulation: even for mathematically complex and geometrically unusual images, they produce detailed, actionable correction sequences. Functions and geometry categories nonetheless pose the greatest challenge, confirming that fine-grained geometric and mathematical perception remains a critical bottleneck for current VLMs—consistent with recent geometric benchmarks. Human validation reveals that automated LLM judges systematically overestimate reconstruction quality, and even the best-aligned judge remains unreliable for episode-level decisions without human recalibration.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: The benchmark comprises 140 episodes across four Describer–Generator pairs (10 per category–difficulty condition)—sufficient for exploratory analysis but modest for robust category-level conclusions and cross-model generalisation; the observed rankings may shift with additional model pairings or larger episode counts. Human annotations are available for a single model pair ( gpt-5.2 + gpt-image-1.5 ), limiting the scope of the human–automated correlation analysis; extending ratings to further pairs would validate whether iterative improvement observed by LLM judges is also perceived by human raters. All prompts and evaluations are in English; the game’s generalisation to other languages is not assessed. The automated judges are themselves subject to the perceptual and linguistic biases of their training data, and their ratings should be interpreted alongside, rather than as a replacement for, human judgements. The benchmark currently covers seven image categories; extending it to broader visual domains, including natural photographs at higher resolution, remains future work.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: All images in the dataset are either synthetically generated or drawn from Visual Genome ( Krishna et al., 2017 ) , a publicly available, consent-collected dataset. No personally identifiable information is present in the stimuli. Annotation tasks were designed to be low-risk and non-sensitive. The generated images produced by the game’s Generator models may contain artefacts or unintended content. Automated evaluation with LLM judges carries the general risk that model-specific biases propagate into benchmark rankings; we mitigate this by using three judges from distinct model families and validating against human ratings. All game transcripts, model outputs, human annotation data, and evaluation code will be publicly released to support reproducible follow-up research.

sections.text: The prompt templates are given in Figure 20 , 21 . The prompt template for generating synthetic images is given in Figure 22 . We used GPT-5.2 for generating the synthetic images. template C.0.1 Let’s play a game. I will feed you an image and you will produce the most accurate description possible. The description should capture every detail and be extremely precise. Your description must be at most 200 tokens long. The output should consist of an initial tag followed by the description. Reply just with the two tags and their related content. template C.0.2 You will now receive an image that was generated using your initial description. The goal is to generate an image as similar as possible to the original one. If you deem that the generated image is close enough to the original one, reply with "". If not, you will reply with the changes needed to correct the image. The updated description should ONLY contain the changes/edits that have to be made to the previous image to make it look like the original image. Do NOT provide the full description again. Your description must be at most 200 tokens long. The output should consist of an initial tag ,followed by the changes or just a tag word if you deem that the images are similar enough. Reply just with the two tags and the content related. Then these steps will repeat until you find the generated image similar enough to the original image. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-SA 4.0 arXiv:2606.01901v1 [cs.CV] 01 Jun 2026 The Image Reconstruction Game: Drawing Common Ground Through Iterative Multimodal Dialogue Sherzod Hakimov Affiliation: Computational Linguistics, Department of LinguisticsUniversity of Potsdam, Germany Email: firstname.lastname@uni-potsdam.de Mattia D’Agostini Affiliation: Computational Linguistics, Department of LinguisticsUniversity of Potsdam, Germany Ivan Samodelkin Affiliation: Computational Linguistics, Department of LinguisticsUniversity of Potsdam, Germany David Schlangen Affiliation: Computational Linguistics, Department of LinguisticsUniversity of Potsdam, Germany Affiliation: German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI), Berlin, Germany Abstract We introduce the Image Reconstruction Game, a fully automated benchmark in which a vision-language model issues corrective instructions to an image generator across multiple turns, making accumulated common ground directly observable as a rendered image. Benchmarking two Describer models crossed with two Generator models across seven image categories, we find that the describer is the dominant factor in reconstruction quality, while the generator determines whether iterative refinement helps or hurts. Mathematical and geometric images pose the greatest challenge. The describer’s token budget strongly affects convergence: shorter budgets yield sparser first renderings with more room for visible improvement, while longer budgets raise absolute quality but leave less to fix. Stronger describers use a richer correction vocabulary spanning spatial, numeric, and structural categories, while weaker describers concentrate on surface properties and tend to stop after a few turns. Human validation shows that the best automated judge reaches only slight-to-fair agreement with human preferences, and automated scores require human recalibration to be used reliably. 1 Introduction Figure 1: In the IR game, one model (the describer) tries to steer another (the generator) towards faithful reproduction of a target, using only natural language descriptions, over several turns. Figure shows example of how the generated image develops in response to the instructions (which are not shown), for three different model pairings and the same target. Figure 2: Overview of the Image Reconstruction Game. The Describer (a VLM) has access to the target image I ∗ I^{*} and communicates with the Generator (an image model) exclusively through natural language. The Generator produces a rendering ( I 1 I_{1} or I 2 I_{2} ) from the accumulated dialogue; the Describer observes both I ∗ I^{*} and the rendering and issues a corrective instruction for the next turn. Each rendering makes the current state of common ground directly visible, and the loop continues until the Describer signals convergence or a turn limit is reached. Comparison is done between target image I ∗ I^{*} and the final turn generated image I T I_{T} . Imagine you have a picture “in your head” – a scene that you saw, a diagram that you think could explain something, etc. – that you want to see materialised. Image generation models aim to address this use case: You describe what is “in your head” using language, and the model generates an image. Where early models technically simply were functions from textual prompts to images, modern models set up this task in a more iterative, incremental and dialogic way, where earlier attempts can be corrected and modified. Using terminology from the study of conversations, this can be described as a process of conversational grounding Clark (1996) , where common ground between the interactants is reached through an interactive process of clarification and correction. This paper uses this setup to test current models on the various components of this task: How good are current language and vision models at describing an image in such a way as to steer an image generation model to reproduce it, and how good are such image generation models at being steered? Figure 1 illustrates the outputs of three model pairs across turns to reconstruct the target image through dialogue. This adds a new dimension to the testing of models that combine linguistic and visual capabilities, as commonly the focus in their evaluation is on non-interactive tasks—captioning, VQA, image–text alignment—that do not test the capacities Shridhar et al. (2020) . Settings such as those used in CoDraw ( Kim et al., 2019 ) establish that iterative visual communication can be studied as a collaborative task with measurable outcomes, but rely on human players and fixed symbolic representations. Conversational image generation systems ( El-Nouby et al., 2019 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) place the human in the describer role, targeting user intent rather than evaluating the describer itself. Neither line holds one component fixed while varying the other, and neither connects communication trajectories to human perceptual judgements of outcomes. We introduce the Image Reconstruction Game , a fully automated multimodal dialogue game that fills these gaps (see Figure 2 ). A describer model (a VLM) observes a target image and must steer an image generator to reproduce it through a sequence of natural-language turns; at each turn the generator’s rendering makes the current state of common ground directly visible, and the describer observes both target and all renderings up to that point in the dialogue before issuing a corrective instruction. No human is in the loop: the game is played entirely between models under controlled, reproducible conditions. This design lets us investigate four research questions: RQ1 Can VLMs detect fine-grained perceptual differences between paired images and verbalise them as actionable, corrective instructions? RQ2 Do those instructions measurably reduce the difference between the target and the current rendering over turns? RQ3 Does the describer–generator pair build common ground progressively, as reflected in both automated similarity scores and human ratings? RQ4 Which automated image-similarity metrics best track human perceptual judgements in this setting? Addressing this last question is non-trivial: embedding-based similarity metrics are known to diverge substantially from human perceptual judgements ( Ghazanfari et al., 2024 ) , and LLM-based judges—while better correlated with human ratings than CLIP or BLIP in text-to-image settings ( Lu et al., 2023 ) —cannot be assumed to carry over to image reconstruction without direct empirical validation ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Marjieh et al., 2024 ) . Our contributions are: (i) a new task formulation and instance set spanning seven image categories that vary the difficulty of perception and verbalisation; (ii) a benchmark comparing two describer models against two generators, isolating describer quality from generator variation; (iii) a human similarity rating study on a stratified subset, together with an analysis of which automated metrics are most reliable proxies; and (iv) a qualitative analysis of what kinds of differences are hard to perceive or verbalise 1 1 1 https://github.com/clp-research/image-reconstruction-game . 2 Related Work CoDraw ( Kim et al., 2019 ) establishes the asymmetric Teller–Drawer paradigm for iterative visual reconstruction through multi-turn dialogue, and related work shows how common ground accumulates across turns when agents describe or identify shared images ( Haber et al., 2019 ; Clark et al., 2021 ; Madureira and Schlangen, 2023 ; Testoni and Fernández, 2024 ; Han and Schlangen, 2017 ) . Game-based frameworks have also been adopted as evaluation instruments for language and multimodal models: Chalamalasetti et al. (2023) systematise this for text-based chat models, and Hakimov et al. (2025) extend it to multimodal models with games probing reference resolution and image comparison ( Zhong et al., 2021 ; Mohapatra, 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Our game inherits this paradigm where players are VLM models as describer and generative image model as generator, making common ground directly observable as a rendered image at every turn. A broad family of systems generates or refines images through multi-turn natural language ( Ullah et al., 2022 ; El-Nouby et al., 2019 ; Lee et al., 2021 ; Wei et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . In all cases a human user provides instructions; the research question is how to build a better generative pipeline, not how to evaluate the instruction-giver. Co-creative drawing agents assist human sketchers in open-ended creative tasks ( Davis et al., 2016 ; Davis et al., 2017 ; Fan et al., 2019 ; Huang et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Ibarrola et al., 2024 ; Davis and Rafner, 2025 ) , while emergent communication research asks whether agents can evolve functional visual protocols through interaction ( Fernando et al., 2020 ; Mihai and Hare, 2021 ; Qiu et al., 2022 ; Vinker et al., 2025 ) . Both treat visual output as a communicative medium, but target artistic expression or protocol emergence rather than the fidelity of reconstruction by existing models. Human evaluation of generated images typically takes the form of pairwise preference judgements or direct similarity ratings, and is used as the ground-truth reference against which automated metrics are calibrated. Standard metrics such as SSIM, LPIPS, DINO, and CLIP are known to diverge from human mid-level perceptual judgements ( Ghazanfari et al., 2024 ) , and multimodal LLMs similarly under-perform humans on explicit visual similarity tasks ( Fu et al., 2024 ) . LipSim ( Ghazanfari et al., 2024 ) and LLMScore ( Lu et al., 2023 ) address this by providing provably robust perceptual similarity estimates and aligning metrics to human quality ratings respectively, while Marjieh et al. (2024) ; Marjieh et al. (2022) show that LLMs can approximate human similarity ratings across perceptual domains, though with systematic biases. We extend this line to image reconstruction, using human ratings to validate LLM judges that also participated as Describer models. Recent benchmarks specifically targeting mathematical and geometric visual perception—including MathOPEval ( Li et al., 2025 ) , GGBench ( Wei et al., 2026 ) , MATHGLANCE ( Sun et al., 2025 ) —consistently show that diagram-level geometric perception is a critical bottleneck in current VLMs. Where these benchmarks measure whether a model can read a geometric figure, the Image Reconstruction Game asks whether a model can articulate residual differences between two such figures—a harder, relational task. Our finding that Functions and Geometry categories pose the greatest challenge aligns with and extends this body of evidence to corrective, goal-directed communication. 3 The Image Reconstruction Game 3.1 Task definition Game description. The Image Reconstruction Game is a two-player dialogue game implemented within the clem framework for game-based model evaluation ( Chalamalasetti et al., 2023 ; Hakimov et al., 2025 ) . In this framework, a programmatic GameMaster instantiates each game episode with a given target image, manages turn-by-turn prompting of the two players, enforces the communication protocol, and records the episode for scoring. The two players occupy asymmetric roles with different information access and capabilities (see Figure 2 ). The Describer is a Vision-and-Language Model that has full access to the target image I ∗ I^{*} . Its goal is to produce natural-language utterances that guide the Generator toward a faithful visual reproduction of I ∗ I^{*} . The Generator is an image generation model that never observes I ∗ I^{*} directly; it can only perceive the accumulated dialogue history—the sequence of Describer utterances—and must render an image conditioned on that text. The game unfolds over multiple turns: at each turn the Describer observes both I ∗ I^{*} and the Generator’s previous rendering I t − 1 I_{t-1} ( t t stands for the turn index), then issues a corrective instruction or signals convergence; the Generator produces a new image based on the dialogue and previous rendering. This iterative structure operationalises the progressive building of common ground ( Alikhani and Stone, 2020 ) : each rendering I t I_{t} is a visible projection of the shared state constructed so far, and each Describer utterance is a grounding act that attempts to reduce the residual gap. The asymmetric information design—where only the Describer knows I ∗ I^{*} — mirrors the Teller–Drawer setup of CoDraw ( Kim et al., 2019 ) and multimodal dialogue games (referential, collaboration, spatial navigation) studied by Hakimov et al. (2025) , while extending them to open-ended natural-language communication with modern generative image models. Capability tested. The game is designed to probe two interleaved capabilities that standard VLM benchmarks Agrawal et al. (2017) ; Yue et al. (2024) do not jointly assess. First, the Describer must perceive fine-grained differences between I ∗ I^{*} and I t − 1 I_{t-1} — a visual discrimination task that is considerably harder than captioning a single image and that demands sensitivity to spatial, metric, and relational properties. Second, it must verbalise those differences as specific corrective instructions for the Generator to act on, which requires goal-directed language production rather than generic scene description. The Generator, in turn, must interpret and act on incremental instructions while maintaining coherence with what has already been rendered. Jointly, these demands test whether a VLM can function as a goal-directed communicative agent in a closed-loop, multimodal setting. 3.2 Prompts and communication protocol Each player’s messages must conform to the communication protocol so that the GameMaster can validate, parse, and relay them between players. An episode continues until one of three stopping criteria is met: (1) Player A signals convergence by producing a done action; (2) the maximum turn limit of T = 10 T{=}10 is reached; or (3) a player violates the protocol. Player A (Describer). Player A is a VLM that receives the target image I ∗ I^{*} and the most recent Generator rendering I t − 1 I_{t-1} at every turn (on turn 1, only I ∗ I^{*} is available, as no rendering exists yet). The GameMaster presents these images with a prompt that asks Player A either to describe I ∗ I^{*} in sufficient detail for an image generator to reproduce it (turn 1), or to identify specific remaining differences between I ∗ I^{*} and I t − 1 I_{t-1} and issue a targeted corrective instruction (turns t > 1 t>1 ). Player A must wrap its output in <DESCRIPTION> … </DESCRIPTION> tags so that the GameMaster can parse and relay the message to Player B; a response consisting solely of done (without tags) signals convergence and ends the episode. A token budget of 200 tokens per turn is imposed to enforce concise, targeted corrections rather than exhaustive re-descriptions. The correction turns place a higher demand on visual reasoning than the initial description: corrections must be relational —specifying what is wrong relative to the current rendering—should focus on what to improve rather than descriptions of the image from scratch. Player B (Generator). Player B is an image generation model that receives two inputs at each turn: the previous rendering I t − 1 I_{t-1} and the text message produced by Player A in the same turn. It does not have access to I ∗ I^{*} at any point; its only signal is the accumulated dialogue history together with the visual context of its own previous output. The GameMaster also passes the full sequence of prior Player A utterances alongside I t − 1 I_{t-1} , ensuring that compositional information established in early turns is not lost when later turns focus on local corrections. Player B’s sole output is a new rendered image I t I_{t} , which is then forwarded to Player A as the basis for the next turn. All prompt templates are given in Appendix C . Figure 3: Representative target images ( hard level) for seven categories in the dataset 4 Experimental Setup 4.1 Models Describer models. We evaluate a set of publicly available VLMs in the Describer role. Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct Yang et al. (2025) was run locally on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU and GPT-5.2 model was accessed via API. A fixed token budget of 200 tokens was used. Generator models. We use two image generation models as generators: Gemini-3.1-nano-banana and GPT-Image-1.5 . Both are accessed via their respective image generation APIs in image-to-image conditioning mode: at each turn the Generator receives the previous rendering I t − 1 I_{t-1} together with the accumulated dialogue history, not merely the latest instruction. Calls are made with default sampling parameters; seeds are not fixed across turns (as neither API exposes turn-level seed control), so observed score changes across turns reflect a combination of conditioning behaviour and sampling stochasticity. Each Describer is evaluated against each Generator, yielding a Describer × \times Generator grid of results; the Generator is held fixed within each grid cell so that outcome differences are attributable to the Describer’s communicative quality rather than to rendering capability. 4.2 Benchmark conditions The benchmark comprises 14 experiment conditions obtained by crossing seven instance categories with two difficulty levels, easy and hard . Each condition contains 10 episodes , yielding 140 episodes in total. The six categories are generated synthetically by prompting an LLM to produce Python code, the code is executed to obtain the target image (see Figure 22 in Appendix C ). Figure 3 shows representative target images. Simple Shapes contain coloured geometric primitives at specified positions; differences are visually salient but require precise spatial and color language. Geometry diagrams depict labelled figures and constructions with subtle metric differences. Functions show mathematical function graphs; differences concern curve shape, scale, and axis labels. Line Graph , Bar Graph , and Pie Graph encode statistical data visually; corrections must be numerically precise. We also use real photographs from the Visual Genome Krishna et al. (2017) dataset to compare the with synthetic categories. Difficulty is defined consistently across synthetic categories: easy instances use fewer elements, simpler structure, and unambiguous layouts, while hard instances introduce additional complexity—more data series, finer geometric detail, denser labelling—that increases both perceptual and verbalisation demands. For Visual Genome, easy instances depict scenes with a small number of salient objects; hard instances are denser and more cluttered. All instances were checked and verified manually (synthetic ones were generated with the complexity included in the prompt and then confirmed, Visual Genome instances were manually selected). Hard instances receive consistently lower mean similarity scores than easy instances across all categories and model pairs (Table 3 , Appendix B ), confirming the intended difficulty ordering. 4.3 Tasks & Evaluation We evaluate episode outcomes using two tasks. Task 1: Pairwise Similarity Judges are shown the target image ( Image A ) and a Generator rendering ( Image B ) and asked to rate their visual and semantic similarity on a 0–10 scale: How similar is Image B to Image A? Image A is the original. Image B was generated by a model. Please rate their overall visual & semantic similarity using the scale below: 0 Completely different image 1–3 Very different; only a few elements in common 4–6 Partial match; some key elements captured, but important differences remain 7–9 Strong match; most elements correct, with minor differences in detail, colour, or placement 10 Identical or indistinguishable Task 2: Triplet Preference Judges are shown the target image alongside two Generator renderings (from the first and the final turns) and asked to select which rendering is more visually similar to the target . This two-alternative forced-choice format abstracts away from absolute scale calibration and directly measures relative reconstruction quality—for example, whether a later-turn rendering is preferred over an earlier one considering the iterative improvement across turns. Human judges. We collect human ratings for both tasks by asking them to annotate all 140 episodes. Each data point in both tasks is rated by three independent annotators with backgrounds in Computational Linguistics and Computer Science (who are also authors). The annotation guidelines and interfaces are given in Appendix A . LLM judges. We use three LLMs as judges for both tasks. GPT-5.2 and Qwen3-VL-30B are drawn from the same model families used in the Describer role, allowing us to examine whether a model’s ratings are consistent with—or systematically biased by—its prior exposure to the task as a generator of descriptions. Self-serving evaluation, in which a model rates its own outputs more favourably than an independent observer would, is a known failure mode of LLM-as-judge pipelines ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Marjieh et al., 2024 ) ; including these models as judges provides a direct test of whether this bias is present in our setting. Claude-4.5 Sonnet was not used in experiments and therefore we included it as an independent, out-of-distribution LLM judge. Comparing the three judges against each other and against human ratings allows us to assess both the overall reliability of LLM-based evaluation in this setting and the degree to which judge scores are confounded by a model’s participation in the task being evaluated. LipSim ( Ghazanfari et al., 2024 ) serves as the automated metric for Task 2; standard alternatives (SSIM, LPIPS, DINO, CLIP) are excluded as they are well-documented to diverge from human mid-level perceptual judgements ( Ghazanfari et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) . LipSim provides a provably robust perceptual similarity distance using Lipschitz-constrained neural networks, offering certified stability under input perturbations. 5 Results and Analysis 5.1 Automated judge calibration Table 1 reports pairwise judge agreement for both evaluation tasks. Figure 4 shows that all three automated judges agree mainly on the overall ranking of model pairs, with gpt-5.2 + gemini-3.1 consistently highest and Qwen3 + gpt-image-1.5 consistently lowest among all judges. The describer is the dominant factor (RQ1) : gpt-5.2 outperforms Qwen-3 by approximately one point across all conditions, with the ranking stable across all three judges. Within each describer, gemini-3.1 yields higher scores than gpt-image-1.5 ( RQ2 ). Category-level results reveal two separable bottlenecks: perception limits scores on Functions and Geometry hard instances (fine-grained details such as curve shapes, axis ticks), while verbalisation is the separate challenge of converting perceived differences into actionable instructions. 5.3 Iterative Refinement The iterative payoff (the difference in scores between the final turn image in comparison to the first turn image) is as follows and address the RQ3 : Δ Q = score I T − score I 1 \Delta_{Q}=\text{score}_{I_{T}}-\text{score}_{I_{1}} . Gemini-3.1 pairings improve across turns; gpt-image-1.5 pairings show near-zero or negative deltas—additional turns degrade rather than improve the reconstruction (Figures 18 and 18 , Appendix B ). The generator also determines whether iterative refinement is beneficial . Figure 5 shows convergence outcomes per pair where each category refers to whether the first turn image has changed in scores in comparison to the final turn one. Qwen3-based pairs produce mostly single-turn episodes, leaving little room for improvement or regression; gpt-5.2 / gpt-image-1.5 continues to the turn limit but still regresses in roughly a third of cases. More turns do not guarantee higher quality (see also Figure 19 , Appendix B ). Among all pairs, gpt-5.2 + gemini-3.1 shows the most consistent per-turn improvement. A shorter budget yields more visibly improved final images: at 10 tokens the first rendering I 1 I_{1} is sparse, so corrections have substantial room to close the gap; at 200 tokens I 1 I_{1} is already detailed, leaving little room for improvement—and more for regression. Absolute final-turn scores increase with budget while triplet preference for the final image decreases because it is easier to tell apart the first rendering from the final when the budget is low (full statistics in Figures 18 and 18 , Appendix B ). This quality–stability trade-off is driven by the starting-point quality of I 1 I_{1} . Figure 6: Convergence outcomes by token budget for gpt-5.2 + gpt-image-1.5 . A shorter budget produces a sparser first rendering, giving corrections more visible room to improve it. 5.5 Correction Language We collected a list of words for respective categories that the describer uses to correct the rendering on subsequent turns. Figure 7 summarises the per-category usage rate per model pair. gpt-5.2 corrections are lexically broad, spanning Label/Text , Numeric , Comparison , and Positive Acknowledgement in addition to the universal Position and Color axes. Qwen3-VL-30B corrections concentrate almost exclusively on Color and Shape , with near-zero Numeric use (GPT-5.2 uses coordinate notation such as x=0 , y=0 ; Qwen3 contributes almost nothing) and zero Positive Acknowledgement . Qwen3-based pairs produce mostly single-turn episodes, so the language profile reflects only the coarsest initial instructions, with no opportunity for the structural and numeric precision that GPT-5.2 develops over longer dialogues (Table 5 : full list of keywords, Figure 14 : top-10 keywords). Human annotators showed moderate mutual agreement: mean r = 0.48 r=0.48 / ρ = 0.49 \rho=0.49 on Task 1 and mean κ = 0.29 \kappa=0.29 on Task 2 (Table 5 , Appendix A ). GPT-5.2 is the most human-aligned judge (RQ4) but still very low for practical applications : Task-1 correlation r = 0.56 r=0.56 is the highest among all automated judges, and Task-2 triplet agreement is κ = 0.22 \kappa=0.22 . All three automated judges are systematically more tolerant than humans: human annotators assign substantially lower mean similarity scores, with Qwen3 showing the largest upward bias. Automated scores require human recalibration before they can be used to set quality thresholds. Qwen3’s near-chance triplet agreement with humans ( κ ≈ 0 \kappa\approx 0 ), despite competitive static benchmark performance, illustrates that game-based probing surfaces failure modes that single-turn evaluation misses. Across all three category types, gpt-5.2 + gemini-3.1 produces the closest renderings; gpt-5.2 + gpt-image-1.5 runs to ten turns but still falls short on fine details. Lower token budgets and Qwen3-based pairs yield semantically weaker reconstructions, with key structural elements missing or substituted. 6 Conclusion We introduced the Image Reconstruction Game, a fully automated multimodal reference game that turns common ground into a directly observable artefact: the rendered image produced after each dialogue turn. Unlike static benchmarks, the game separately measures two distinct model competencies—the ability to perceive and verbalise residual differences (Describer), and the ability to incorporate targeted corrections without losing prior progress (Generator). Our experiments show that describer quality is the dominant factor in reconstruction fidelity, while the generator determines whether multi-turn interaction provides any benefit at all. Notably, stronger VLMs are capable of fine-grained visual articulation: even for mathematically complex and geometrically unusual images, they produce detailed, actionable correction sequences. Functions and geometry categories nonetheless pose the greatest challenge, confirming that fine-grained geometric and mathematical perception remains a critical bottleneck for current VLMs—consistent with recent geometric benchmarks. Human validation reveals that automated LLM judges systematically overestimate reconstruction quality, and even the best-aligned judge remains unreliable for episode-level decisions without human recalibration. Limitations The benchmark comprises 140 episodes across four Describer–Generator pairs (10 per category–difficulty condition)—sufficient for exploratory analysis but modest for robust category-level conclusions and cross-model generalisation; the observed rankings may shift with additional model pairings or larger episode counts. Human annotations are available for a single model pair ( gpt-5.2 + gpt-image-1.5 ), limiting the scope of the human–automated correlation analysis; extending ratings to further pairs would validate whether iterative improvement observed by LLM judges is also perceived by human raters. All prompts and evaluations are in English; the game’s generalisation to other languages is not assessed. The automated judges are themselves subject to the perceptual and linguistic biases of their training data, and their ratings should be interpreted alongside, rather than as a replacement for, human judgements. The benchmark currently covers seven image categories; extending it to broader visual domains, including natural photographs at higher resolution, remains future work. Ethics Statement All images in the dataset are either synthetically generated or drawn from Visual Genome ( Krishna et al., 2017 ) , a publicly available, consent-collected dataset. No personally identifiable information is present in the stimuli. Annotation tasks were designed to be low-risk and non-sensitive. The generated images produced by the game’s Generator models may contain artefacts or unintended content. Automated evaluation with LLM judges carries the general risk that model-specific biases propagate into benchmark rankings; we mitigate this by using three judges from distinct model families and validating against human ratings. All game transcripts, model outputs, human annotation data, and evaluation code will be publicly released to support reproducible follow-up research. References Agrawal et al.
